subject: physics

items.q: In which of these situations does the force described make the object rotate?
items.correct: A push on the edge of a door, away from its hinges
items.misconception: A push on a door aimed straight through its hinges
items.why: Students treat the moment as a property of the force alone rather than of the force and its position together, so they cannot accept that a large force could have no turning effect at all. The moment is force × perpendicular distance. If the line of action passes through the pivot, d = 0, so M = F × 0 = 0 Nm however large F is. This is why pushing a door at the hinge edge does not open it.
items.random_wrong: Two equal pushes on opposite faces of a still box

items.q: A cyclist pushes vertically down on one pedal. Which statement best describes what this single force does?
items.correct: It has a turning effect on the pedal crank about the axle
items.misconception: It cannot turn the crank because it is only one force
items.why: The clearest images of turning that students meet are two-handed ones - steering wheels, taps, screw tops - so they generalise that turning always needs a pair of forces, and earlier work on resultant forces has trained them to think of a single force as producing straight-line motion. The specification states that a force or a system of forces may cause an object to rotate. One force is enough, provided it acts at some perpendicular distance from the pivot: a single push on the edge of a door swings it about its hinges.
items.random_wrong: It turns the crank only when it acts through the axle

items.q: A force acts on a bar that can turn about a pivot. What is the turning effect of that force called?
items.correct: Its moment about that pivot
items.misconception: Its resultant force at the pivot
items.why: The word 'turning force' is used loosely in class, and students have met 'per' units such as N/kg and m/s, so a compound unit is assumed to be a division rather than a multiplication. A moment is not a force; it is the turning effect of a force. The equation multiplies, so the unit multiplies too: newtons × metres = newton-metres, Nm. A unit of N/m would mean the equation was force ÷ distance, which it is not.
items.random_wrong: Its lever arm from the pivot

items.q: The size of the moment of a force is defined by which equation?
items.correct: moment of a force = force × distance
items.misconception: moment of a force = force ÷ distance
items.why: The word 'turning force' is used loosely in class, and students have met 'per' units such as N/kg and m/s, so a compound unit is assumed to be a division rather than a multiplication. A moment is not a force; it is the turning effect of a force. The equation multiplies, so the unit multiplies too: newtons × metres = newton-metres, Nm. A unit of N/m would mean the equation was force ÷ distance, which it is not.
items.random_wrong: moment of a force = force × bar length

items.q: Which row gives the correct units to use in M = F d?
items.correct: M in Nm, F in N, d in m
items.misconception: M in Nm, F in N, d in cm
items.why: Unit conversion feels like an optional tidying-up step rather than part of the physics, and the arithmetic with whole centimetres is easier, so students leave the figure alone and add the unit at the end. The specification states that d is in metres. Convert every distance to metres before substituting, or the answer is a hundred times too large. 15 cm = 0.15 m, so M = 40 N × 0.15 m = 6.0 Nm.
items.random_wrong: M in Nm, F in kg, d in m

items.q: In the equation M = F d, what exactly does the distance d mean?
items.correct: The perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action
items.misconception: The distance from the pivot to the point where the force acts
items.why: In every introductory example the force is applied at right angles to the bar, so the perpendicular distance and the distance along the bar happen to be equal. Students take the shortcut as the definition and never notice the word 'perpendicular'. The specification defines d as the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force. Extend the force's line of action, then measure the shortest (perpendicular) distance from the pivot to that line. Only when the force is at right angles to the bar do the two distances agree.
items.random_wrong: The distance the object moves as the force turns it round

items.q: A spanner is 0.30 m long. A 50 N force is applied at its end, but at an angle, so the perpendicular distance from the nut to the line of action of the force is 0.24 m. What is the moment about the nut?
items.correct: 12 Nm
items.misconception: 15 Nm
items.why: In every introductory example the force is applied at right angles to the bar, so the perpendicular distance and the distance along the bar happen to be equal. Students take the shortcut as the definition and never notice the word 'perpendicular'. The specification defines d as the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force. Extend the force's line of action, then measure the shortest (perpendicular) distance from the pivot to that line. Only when the force is at right angles to the bar do the two distances agree.
items.random_wrong: 208 Nm

items.q: A force of 25 N acts at a perpendicular distance of 0.20 m from a pivot. What is the moment of the force about the pivot?
items.correct: 5.0 Nm
items.misconception: 125 Nm
items.why: The word 'turning force' is used loosely in class, and students have met 'per' units such as N/kg and m/s, so a compound unit is assumed to be a division rather than a multiplication. A moment is not a force; it is the turning effect of a force. The equation multiplies, so the unit multiplies too: newtons × metres = newton-metres, Nm. A unit of N/m would mean the equation was force ÷ distance, which it is not.

items.q: A force of 40 N acts at a perpendicular distance of 15 cm from a pivot. What is the moment of the force?
items.correct: 6.0 Nm
items.misconception: 600 Nm
items.why: Unit conversion feels like an optional tidying-up step rather than part of the physics, and the arithmetic with whole centimetres is easier, so students leave the figure alone and add the unit at the end. The specification states that d is in metres. Convert every distance to metres before substituting, or the answer is a hundred times too large. 15 cm = 0.15 m, so M = 40 N × 0.15 m = 6.0 Nm.
items.random_wrong: 2.7 Nm

items.q: An object is balanced about a pivot. Which statement must be true?
items.correct: The total clockwise moment equals the total anticlockwise moment
items.misconception: The biggest force on one side matches the biggest on the other
items.why: The two-force see-saw is the only case students have practised, so with three forces they fall back on comparing forces directly instead of totalling moments. The specification refers to the total clockwise moment and the total anticlockwise moment. Each force gets its own moment, F × d, and the moments acting in the same sense are added before the two totals are compared.
items.random_wrong: The pivot must be at the exact centre of the balanced object

items.q: A beam is balanced on a pivot. A 300 N weight hangs 1.2 m to the left of the pivot, and a single weight hangs 0.8 m to the right. What is the weight on the right?
items.why: The symmetrical case is the one students meet first and the one that matches the everyday word 'balanced', so equal forces at equal distances becomes the mental picture of balance. Balance is a condition on moments, not on forces. The total clockwise moment equals the total anticlockwise moment, so a lighter child sitting further out balances a heavier child sitting closer in.

items.q: A rod is balanced on a pivot. A 6.0 N force acts 0.50 m from the pivot on one side. A 4.0 N force acts on the other side. How far from the pivot is the 4.0 N force?
items.why: Classroom see-saws and metre rules are usually pivoted at the centre for convenience, so symmetry becomes part of students' definition of balance rather than a feature of the particular example. Balance requires equal total clockwise and anticlockwise moments about whichever pivot is used. A wheelbarrow, a crowbar and a nutcracker are all balanced or in equilibrium with the pivot at one end, nowhere near the centre.

items.q: A rule balances with a 2 N weight 30 cm to the left of the pivot and a 3 N weight 20 cm to the right. The 2 N weight is replaced by a 3 N weight in the same place. Which single change will rebalance the rule?
items.correct: Move the 3 N weight on the left to 20 cm from the pivot
items.misconception: Move the 3 N weight on the left to 45 cm from the pivot
items.why: Students read the size of the force as the whole story and treat distance as a detail, so 'stronger force wins' feels like common sense until they use the equation. The moment is force × distance, so the two must trade off. On a balanced object the smaller force sits at the greater distance: 6.0 N × 0.50 m = 4.0 N × 0.75 m, both giving 3.0 Nm.
items.random_wrong: Leave both weights as they are: the forces now match

items.q: What do a simple lever and a simple gear system have in common?
items.correct: Both are used to transmit the rotational effects of forces
items.misconception: Both create extra energy to make a bigger turning effect
items.why: The output force really is bigger than the input force, which looks like something has been created, and students have no other explanation for where the gain comes from. A lever transmits the rotational effect of a force. At balance the moment of the effort equals the moment of the load, so a small effort at a large distance gives the same moment as a large load force at a small distance. The moment is passed on, not increased.
items.random_wrong: Both turn a rotation into a straight-line push instead

items.q: A gardener pushes down on the far end of a long spade handle to lever up a lump of soil. Why does this make the job easier?
items.correct: The force acts further from the pivot, so its moment is larger
items.misconception: The longer handle makes the pushing force itself become larger
items.why: Students feel the job get easier and attribute that to a change in the force, because force is the quantity they know best. The idea that the same force can have different effects depending on where it acts is new. The force you apply is unchanged; what changes is d. Because M = F d, doubling the distance from the pivot doubles the moment, which is what loosens the nut.
items.random_wrong: The lever gives out a bigger moment than the one put into it

items.q: Two gear wheels are meshed together. The first gear is turned clockwise. How does the second gear turn?
items.correct: Anticlockwise, as their teeth push each other the other way
items.misconception: Clockwise, as the turning effect is passed straight along
items.why: Students picture the rotation being 'handed on' unchanged, as it is by a chain or a belt on the same side, and do not track what the teeth actually do at the point of contact. Follow the teeth at the meshing point: as one gear's tooth moves down on that side, it drives the other gear's tooth down on its own side, which is the opposite sense of rotation. Two directly meshed gears always turn in opposite directions.
items.random_wrong: It stays still until the first gear has turned fully around

items.q: A small gear drives a larger gear meshed with it. Compared with the small gear, the larger gear turns:
items.correct: more slowly, and with a larger moment
items.misconception: more quickly, and with a larger moment
items.why: 'Bigger' is read as 'more powerful and therefore faster', and the fact that meshed gears move together at the teeth is wrongly extended to mean they complete rotations together. The teeth move at the same speed where the gears mesh, but the larger gear has to move more teeth to complete one turn, so it rotates more slowly. In exchange, the force at its teeth acts at a greater distance from its axle, so it exerts a larger moment.
items.random_wrong: more slowly, and with a smaller moment

items.q: A force of 60 N is applied to a door along a line of action that passes exactly through the hinge. What is the moment of this force about the hinge?
items.correct: Zero, because the perpendicular distance from the hinge is zero
items.misconception: 60 Nm, because a force that large must turn the door somehow
items.why: Students treat the moment as a property of the force alone rather than of the force and its position together, so they cannot accept that a large force could have no turning effect at all. The moment is force × perpendicular distance. If the line of action passes through the pivot, d = 0, so M = F × 0 = 0 Nm however large F is. This is why pushing a door at the hinge edge does not open it.
items.random_wrong: 60 N, because the moment is just the force that is applied

items.q: A 2.0 kg bag hangs from a beam at a perpendicular distance of 0.30 m from the pivot. Gravitational field strength is 9.8 N/kg. What is the moment of the bag's weight about the pivot?
items.correct: 5.9 Nm
items.why: Everyday language uses 'weight' for the reading of a kitchen scale in kilograms, so students see no distinction between the mass in kg and the downward force in N. The specification states that F is a force in newtons. The turning effect of a hanging object is caused by its weight, so convert first using weight = mass × gravitational field strength, then substitute the weight in newtons.
items.random_wrong: 588 Nm

items.q: A plank pivots at its centre. On the left, a 10 N weight sits 0.40 m from the pivot and a 20 N weight sits 0.20 m from it. A single weight placed 0.50 m to the right balances the plank. What is that weight?
items.why: The two-force see-saw is the only case students have practised, so with three forces they fall back on comparing forces directly instead of totalling moments. The specification refers to the total clockwise moment and the total anticlockwise moment. Each force gets its own moment, F × d, and the moments acting in the same sense are added before the two totals are compared.

items.q: A moment works out as 5.0 newton-metres. Can it be written as 5.0 joules?
items.correct: No. A moment is quoted in newton-metres, Nm; joules are used for work done and energy transferred, which is a different quantity.
items.misconception: Work done is force × distance and a moment is force × distance, so they are the same thing and either unit will do.
items.why: The two equations look identical in words, and students have been told that 1 joule = 1 newton-metre in the context of work done, so they assume the quantities must be interchangeable. The distances mean different things: in work done it is the distance moved along the line of action, while in a moment it is the perpendicular distance from the pivot to that line. Nothing has to move for a moment to exist. The specification gives the moment of a force in newton-metres, Nm.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A gear turns more slowly than the one driving it. Is its turning effect smaller?
items.correct: No. The larger, slower gear exerts a larger moment about its axle, because the force at its teeth acts at a greater distance from that axle.
items.misconception: If it is turning more slowly it must be doing less, so the moment must be smaller as well.
items.why: Speed is the visible quantity, so students use it as a proxy for how much turning effect there is, and have not separated rate of rotation from moment. Rate of rotation and moment are different quantities. Going from a small driving gear to a larger driven gear reduces the rate of rotation but increases the moment, because M = F d and the distance from the axle to the teeth is greater on the larger gear.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
